summary: This document describes Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT), a protocol for delivering multicast traffic from sources in a multicast-enabled network to receivers that lack multicast connectivity to it. It uses UDP encapsulation and unicast replication to reach those receivers.

eli5.summary: Group broadcasts do not work on every network. This sets up a tunnel so a receiver can still get the show, by wrapping it up and sending it individually.

questions: how to receive multicast without multicast support
what udp port does amt use
how does amt work through nat
subtitle: A way to deliver multicast to receivers behind networks that cannot carry it, by tunneling it over UDP.

tldr.problem: Many receivers sit in networks with no multicast connectivity to the network that carries the source, so they cannot receive multicast traffic natively.
tldr.mechanism: A gateway near the receiver asks a relay in a multicast-enabled network for traffic using tunneled IGMP or MLD messages. The relay replicates each multicast packet and sends it to the gateway inside a unicast UDP datagram.
tldr.outcome: Receivers get SSM and ASM traffic with few changes to existing infrastructure, at the price of unicast replication, which the RFC says is no substitute for native multicast under high traffic.

today: RFC 7450 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8777, which changes relay discovery, and by RFC 9601; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem and Where AMT Fits
sections.content:
Multicast suits media broadcasting, video conferencing, real-time data feeds, software updates and more. But many would-be receivers lack multicast connectivity to the networks that carry the sources, mostly because of service provider policies and network limitations.

Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) uses UDP encapsulation to get around this. It lets sites, hosts or applications without native multicast request and receive both Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) and Any-Source Multicast (ASM) traffic from a network that does have connectivity to the source.

The RFC sets limits. It does not cover sourcing multicast from isolated sites. It is not a substitute for native multicast, especially where traffic flow is high, because unicast replication costs more bandwidth. It is meant to be deployed at the border of networks with native multicast, where the AMT service provider can manage access and provisioning.
sections.eli5: If your street has no mail truck for group letters, a helper at the post office makes a separate copy for you and delivers it in a plain envelope.

sections.title: Gateways and Relays
sections.content:
AMT is client-server. A gateway sits in a network that lacks multicast and asks for specific traffic. A relay sits in a multicast-enabled network that contains, or connects to, the sources, and sends the requested traffic back.

AMT leans on existing group management. The gateway runs the host side of IGMP and MLD, and the relay runs the router side. Their messages travel inside AMT control messages as complete IP datagrams, and multicast datagrams travel inside AMT data messages. All AMT messages go over unicast UDP/IP. Each side is described as having a logical pseudo-interface where the encapsulation happens.

To find a relay, the RFC calls for anycast addressing. Relays advertise a route to the same prefix (for example via BGP), and a gateway sends a discovery message to an address in it. That reaches the topologically nearest relay, which answers with its own unicast address. Gateways are not required to use this discovery, but all relay implementations must support it.

The RFC adds a congestion warning: neither AMT nor UDP provides congestion control, so providers are expected to deploy relays near their network border and limit relay address advertisements to those edges.
sections.eli5: The gateway is the kid who asks for a show, and the relay is the helper who has the TV signal. The kid shouts to the nearest helper, and the helper then sends the show over in a private message.

sections.title: Discovery, Membership and Teardown
sections.content:
Discovery. The gateway sends a Relay Discovery message with a random nonce. The responder returns a Relay Advertisement copying the nonce and carrying a relay's unicast address, and the gateway checks the nonce before using that address.

Membership. A relay does not send unsolicited queries to gateways, because the set of gateways may be unknown and large. Instead the gateway sends a Request with a nonce; the relay answers with a Membership Query carrying the nonce, a message authentication code (MAC) and an encapsulated IGMPv3 or MLDv2 General Query. The gateway passes the query to its IGMP or MLD code and sends the resulting reports in Membership Update messages that echo the nonce and MAC. The relay recomputes the MAC from the source address, source port, nonce and a private secret, and ignores the update if it does not match. The query interval in the General Query sets a timer that triggers the next Request.

This three-way handshake means spoofed Request or Membership Update messages cannot make the relay allocate state. A relay allocates tunnel state only when a report creates at least one group subscription.

Teardown. If the gateway's address or port changes (a new DHCP lease, roaming, or a NAT mapping change), the relay may keep sending to the old address. The optional Teardown message lets the gateway ask the relay to stop. Gateway support is RECOMMENDED, but the RFC leaves timeouts and retransmission to implementations; it suggests, for example, retransmitting a Relay Discovery with random exponential back-off, from an initial timeout of 1 second up to 120 seconds.
sections.eli5: First you find a helper. Then you show a secret code the helper gave you, so nobody can pretend to be you. If you move house, you tell the helper to stop sending things to your old address.

sections.title: The Seven AMT Messages
sections.content:
AMT defines seven message types, each sent as a single UDP datagram. Every message starts with a 4-bit version (always 0) and a 4-bit type. Reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt. The destination port of messages sent to a relay is the AMT port, 2268.

Notable fields:

  • Nonces are 32-bit random values: the Discovery Nonce and the Request Nonce.
  • The Request has a P flag: 0 means the relay must reply with an IPv4 packet carrying an IGMPv3 General Query, 1 means an IPv6 packet carrying an MLDv2 General Query.
  • The Membership Query has an L flag (the relay is not accepting updates from new gateway tunnel endpoints), a G flag (gateway address fields are present), a 48-bit Response MAC, the Request Nonce and the encapsulated query. If G is set, a Gateway Port Number and a 16-byte Gateway IP Address follow; an IPv4 address is stored with 96 leading zero bits.
  • The Membership Update carries the Response MAC, the Request Nonce and an encapsulated IGMP or MLD report or leave.
  • Multicast Data carries one complete multicast IP datagram or fragment.
  • Teardown carries the Response MAC, Request Nonce and gateway address and port from an earlier Membership Query.

Most messages MUST carry a valid, non-zero UDP checksum. Multicast Data is the exception: the checksum MAY be zero over IPv4 and SHOULD be valid and non-zero over IPv6 if possible.
sections.eli5: There are seven kinds of notes. Some say "find me a helper", some say "here is my code", and one carries the actual show.

sections.title: Tunnels, NAT and Packet Size
sections.content:
From the relay's point of view, a tunnel is identified by the IP address and UDP port to which it sends encapsulated multicast datagrams. That address is taken from the source address and port of the Membership Update as it arrives, so a NAT in between is handled automatically: replies go to whatever address the NAT produced. The periodic updates also keep the NAT mapping from expiring. A tunnel exists once a report creates group subscriptions, and ends when the last one is removed, when a Teardown arrives, or when the relay's timers expire.

The encapsulated packets need not use the same IP version as the AMT messages: IPv4 AMT messages may carry IPv6/MLD and the other way round.

Fragmentation is a concern because many streaming applications send independent packets and do not want them fragmented. The relay computes a Tunnel MTU by subtracting the IP, UDP and AMT headers from the Path MTU, using either a fixed configured value or ICMP-driven discovery. If a multicast IPv4 datagram is too big and has the DF bit set, the relay MUST discard it and, for SSM sources, send an ICMP Destination Unreachable. If DF is clear, the relay MUST fragment it and encapsulate each fragment. For IPv6 the relay MUST discard the packet and, for SSM sources, send a Packet Too Big message.
sections.eli5: The helper mails the show to whatever return address it sees on your last note, even if a mail room in between changed the label. Packets that are too big for the envelope get cut into pieces or sent back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AMT is not intended to be strongly secure. It gives about the same security as UDP, IGMP and MLD: no delivery or integrity guarantees, and no confidentiality, so groups, sources and streams are sent in the clear. The three-way handshake provides only trivial source authentication, and gives no defense against an eavesdropper or man-in-the-middle.

Relays can still be flooded with Request or Membership Update messages that force MAC computation, though not state allocation. Implementations should limit tunnels per gateway address and joins per tunnel. A relay that withdraws its anycast advertisement when full lets gateways reach the next nearest relay, but the RFC warns this can also let an attack travel from one relay to the next, so advertisements can be confined to administrative routing domains. Forged ICMP messages can distort Path MTU, so relays MUST have a way to disable Path MTU adjustment.

An eavesdropper who captures a nonce and MAC can send spoofed Membership Update or Teardown messages to the relay. Gateways should filter Multicast Data that does not come from the expected relay. A rogue router or AS could also announce a bogus route to the discovery prefix, so network managers must guarantee the integrity of that routing. The relay's private secret SHOULD be changed periodically, with a RECOMMENDED maximum interval of 2 hours, and the prior secret MUST be kept for verifying recent MACs.
sections.eli5: The secret code stops strangers from lying about who they are, but the show is not locked in a box. Anyone who can see the mail can read it.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned two prefixes for anycast discovery of public relays: 192.52.193.0/24 for IPv4 and 2001:3::/32 for IPv6, both named AMT and allocated in 2014-12. A Relay Discovery Address is made by setting the low-order octet of the prefix address to 1; the rest of each prefix is reserved for future use. Public relays must advertise a route to the prefix and answer on that address.

UDP port 2268 was reserved with IANA for AMT, and IANA updated the assignee, contact and reference fields for it to point to this document.
sections.eli5: The address book gave AMT a special set of addresses to call for help, and one door number (port 2268) to knock on.

messages.label: Relay Discovery
messages.note: Carries a random nonce to the Relay Discovery Address.

messages.label: Relay Advertisement
messages.note: Echoes the nonce and gives the relay's unicast address.

messages.label: Membership Query
messages.note: Nonce, MAC and an IGMPv3 or MLDv2 General Query.

messages.label: Membership Update
messages.note: Echoes nonce and MAC with an IGMP or MLD report.

messages.label: Multicast Data
messages.note: Encapsulated multicast packets for subscribed groups.

items.label: Relay Discovery
items.desc: Gateway asks for a relay address.

items.label: Membership Query
items.desc: Relay sends nonce, MAC and a General Query.

items.label: Membership Update
items.desc: Gateway sends an IGMP or MLD report or leave.

items.label: Multicast Data
items.desc: Relay delivers an encapsulated multicast packet.

items.label: Teardown
items.desc: Gateway asks the relay to stop sending to a tunnel endpoint.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the gateway, ignored by the relay.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: 0 asks for an IGMPv3 query, 1 for an MLDv2 query.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the gateway, ignored by the relay.

fields.name: Request Nonce
fields.desc: Random value used to compute the Response MAC and match the reply.
